subject: mathematics
question_text: If f: A→B is a bijective function then prove that (i) fof⁻¹ = I_B (ii) f⁻¹of = I_A.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.15 — LAQ chapter 1 Functions, question 4. The 3+4 split is printed in that book's margin; appearance years are printed board-split as TS 16,18,19 and AP 15,17 — the most-asked question in this chapter across both boards. Publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. Lines naming an identity function use render:'katex' (a capital-letter subscript has no Unicode form). Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Proof that fof⁻¹ = I_B.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove that f composed with its inverse gives the identity — both ways round, and how each one goes.

steps.label: Write what is given
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. The one fact both parts need is that f is a bijection, so f⁻¹ exists and is itself a bijection. Write that before either part.
steps.memory_tip: f is a bijection, so f⁻¹ exists and runs B→A. Say that before either part.
lines: f: A→B is a bijective function,
so f⁻¹: B→A is also a bijection.

lines.text: I_A : A \to A, \quad I_B : B \to B
\text{To prove: } f \circ f^{-1} = I_B \text{ and } f^{-1} \circ f = I_A

recall.must_convey: That f is a bijection, which is why f⁻¹ exists at all and is also a bijection from B to A. Naming f⁻¹ without saying it exists because f is a bijection is partial.
accept: f is a bijection so the inverse exists and goes from B to A and is also a bijection
since f is one one and onto f inverse is defined from B back to A
given f is bijective therefore f inverse exists as a bijection
f bijection kabatti f inverse untundi B nunchi A ki
the inverse function exists because f is a bijection

steps.why: Only a bijection has an inverse function. If f were not onto, some b in B would have nothing to send back, and f⁻¹(b) would be undefined.
common_mistakes: Using f⁻¹ without first saying it exists because f is a bijection.
Writing f⁻¹: A→B — the inverse runs the other way.

steps.label: f after f inverse
steps.margin_note: Four of the eight marks. This side starts at B, so the element you take is b, not a. Get the domain line down, then the substitution.
steps.memory_tip: This side starts at B, so take b, not a. It lands on I_B, whose domain is B.

lines.text: f^{-1} : B \to A \text{ and } f : A \to B
\therefore f \circ f^{-1} : B \to B, \ I_B : B \to B
So both sides have the same domain B.

recall.must_convey: Take b in B, f⁻¹ sends it to the a with f(a) = b, then f sends that a back to b — which is exactly what I_B does. The starting element must be b.
accept: take b in B then f inverse of b is a and f of a is b so the composition gives b which is I B of b
start from b go back with f inverse and forward with f and you return to b
f of f inverse of b equals b so the composition is the identity on B
b teeskoni f inverse tho a vasthundi f tho malli b vasthundi so identity on B
it returns every b to itself so it is I B

steps.why: f⁻¹ undoes f, so doing f⁻¹ then f returns you to where you started. Which identity you land on depends on which set you started in — here you started in B.
common_mistakes: Starting from a in A on this side, which lands on the wrong identity.
Writing I_A instead of I_B for a composition whose domain is B.
Saying 'they cancel' instead of showing f[f⁻¹(b)] = b.

steps.label: f inverse after f
steps.margin_note: Four of the eight marks. The mirror of part (i): this side starts at A, so take a, and it lands on I_A. Write it out fully, never 'by symmetry'.
steps.memory_tip: The mirror: this side starts at A, take a, and it lands on I_A. Write it out — never 'by symmetry'.

lines.text: f : A \to B \text{ and } f^{-1} : B \to A
\therefore f^{-1} \circ f : A \to A, \ I_A : A \to A
So both sides have the same domain A.

recall.must_convey: Take a in A, f sends it to b, then f⁻¹ sends b back to a — which is what I_A does. The starting element must be a, and the result must be I_A, not I_B.
accept: take a in A then f of a is b and f inverse of b is a so the composition gives a which is I A of a
start from a go forward with f and back with f inverse and you return to a
f inverse of f of a equals a so this composition is the identity on A
a teeskoni f tho b vasthundi f inverse tho malli a vasthundi so identity on A
every a comes back to itself so it is I A

steps.why: Same undoing, opposite order — and the order decides which set you start and finish in, so this half lands on I_A. That is why the two parts are marked separately.
common_mistakes: Writing 'by symmetry' and stopping — the examiner marks this part on its own.
Ending at f⁻¹(b) without saying it equals a, so the identity is never reached.
Swapping I_A and I_B between the two parts.

steps.label: Conclude
steps.margin_note: No separate mark. Both results on the final line, in the order the question asked.
steps.memory_tip: Both results on the final line, in the order the question asked.

lines.text: f \circ f^{-1} = I_B, \quad f^{-1} \circ f = I_A

recall.must_convey: Both results together: f after f⁻¹ is the identity on B, and f⁻¹ after f is the identity on A.
accept: f composed with f inverse is I B and f inverse composed with f is I A
both compositions are identities one on B and one on A
hence we get the identity on B and the identity on A
rendu results I B and I A
the two compositions give the two identity functions

steps.why: The question asked for two results. Writing both on the last line shows you finished the second part, which is where four of the eight marks are.
common_mistakes: Writing only one of the two results.
